newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Zinc smelters face lower fee as supplies drop.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Zinc smelters face lower fee as supplies drop.

text.p: Zinc smelters may be on the verge of agreeing to sharp reductions in treatment charges this year, industry sources said on Tuesday.
Few, if any, deals have been struck yet, but many smelters have tempered their expectations in recent weeks given prospects of less material coming their way in 1997, the sources said.

A shortfall in supplies of concentrates -- brought on by an unforeseen series of mine curtailments due to weak refined zinc prices -- also threatens to leave some smelters operating below their maximum capacities, the sources said.
By some estimates, the smelters are steeling to accept fees of below US$170 a tonne, based on a zinc price of US$1,000 a tonne, down from last year's average of US$190 a tonne.
"It's between US$165 (a tonne) where the miners stand and US$175 where the smelters stand," a negotiator for an Asian smelter said.
Final terms are unlikely to be reached before representatives from both sides meet in February for an industry conference in Scottsdale, Arizona.
The big Australian miners, such as Pasminco Ltd and MIM Holdings Ltd, are still in negotiations and hope to finalise 1997 terms at the meeting, sources have confirmed.
Miners and smelters have been as far apart as nearly US$40 a tonne, although representatives from both camps admit to overestimating their positions in the early stages of negotiations.
"Basically, US$190 last year was unrealistic and based on forecasted supplies of concentrates that never materialised," the source said.
"We think US$175 is a more realistic jumping off point at which to negotiate for 1997," he added.
Current spot charges of only around US$150 a tonne support their claim, the miners have maintained.
The miners' position is being further aided by expectations for more smelter capacity as concentrate supplies taper off.
The largest expansion will occur in Korea, where Korea Zinc Co Ltd is planning an 80,000-tonne-a-year increase at its Onsan smelter, taking yearly capacity to 300,000 tonnes.
In Thailand, Padaeng Industry Plc intends to run at an expanded capacity 105,000 tonne in March, up from 73,000 tonnes.
In Brazil, Paraibuna Co's Juiz de Fora smelter is adding 30,000 tonnes of capacity and Cia Mineira de Metais is lifting its capabilities by the same amount.
By the end of this year, the expansion of some smelters should lift Western world capacity to 6.285 million tonnes in 1998 from 6.012 at the start of 1997, broker J.B. Were and Son estimates.
A forecasted supply deficit in concentrates of 29,000 tonnes in 1996 is seen growing to 167,000 tonnes in 1997, J.B. Were figures show.

The broker believes Canada's Noranda Inc produced only about 215,000 tonnes of zinc in 1996 against a previous estimate of 280,000 tonnes, due to severe geotechnical problems. It sees the lower level of production being maintained in 1997.
Closure of the Inmet Mining Corp mine in Tunisia, wiping out 40,000 tonnes per year of concentrates and cut backs elsewhere have caused further tightening in the market.
The shutdown of Anvil Range Mining Corp's for three months from December 20, 1996 due to low zinc prices also is a factor working in favour of the miners.

Stockpiles of ore at the mine are being treated faster than previously anticipated and there is some talk the mine may not be re-opened on schedule due to metallurgiccal difficulties and equipment problems, the sources said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
